#7923. 14 Things You Can Do Now to Prepare for a Power Outage in Winter

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Jennifer Noonan, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 16, 2026 5:18 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Power outages can be difficult to weather any time of year, but not having a working heater when temperatures are frigid can be hard on you and your home. When there’s a winter storm in the forecast, there’s no time to lose. If you start preparing for inclement weather now, even before there’s a whisper about bad weather, and you’ll be in better shape should blizzards, nor’easters, or bomb cyclones head your way.

Make sure you have a good supply of batteries (and if they’re rechargeable batteries, ensure that they’re fully charged!) in a range of sizes for all your emergency needs. Have spares ready for flashlights and radios as well as for smoke detectors, clocks, and other necessities that can run on battery backup.

How many times have you clicked on several flashlights in your junk drawer before finding one that actually works? Carefully test each of your flashlights and figure out which ones work and which don’t. Refresh the batteries and test them again, ditching the flashlights that still don’t work. Purchase additional flashlights if you need them (can you really have too many?). Make sure there’s a “good” light for each member of the family, at the very least. Don’t plan on using candles; flashlights are safer.

Always top off your cars’ fuel tanks when you’re expecting a big storm. Gas station pumps run on electricity and if the power goes out, you won’t be able to get gasoline. If you have a gas-powered portable generator, fill some gas cans, too, so you can keep the generator going.

A key component of a winter survival kit is a means of charging your mobile phone in your car, whether that’s a car charger for your phone or the right cord to connect auto to phone. With a full gas tank and a car charger, you’ll be able to keep your phone working even if you lose power for an extended period of time. You may also want to invest in a solar phone charger, which would allow you to charge your phone without sitting in your driveway.

If you have landline telephone service, it’s worth keeping an old corded landline phone around. Modern phones that plug into wall outlets will not work during a power outage, and having access to a usable landline will help you conserve your cell phone battery.

If the power goes out during winter, how will you keep warm? Devise a plan now, before you’re in that situation. Even a gas-powered furnace requires electricity to run the fan that sends warm air through the vents. If you have a gas fireplace, consider installing a battery backup for the starter if you don’t already have one. If you rely on a wood stove for heat, stock up on firewood. Do not use a propane heater inside the home unless it is one specifically designed for indoor use; carbon monoxide can build up and create a deadly hazard.

Mr. Heater’s Portable Buddy Heater quickly heats up to 225 sq. ft. of space and has a tip-over safety mechanism. Read the review.

When a heavy storm is in the forecast, stock up on drinking water, and fill up the bathtub and washing machine so you’ll have enough water for washing and for flushing the toilets. The PennState extension service says Americans use 50 to 100 gallons of water per person per day, but that kind of stockpile may be hard to achieve in an emergency situation. You will want to have on hand at least a gallon of potable water per person per day.

If your home relies on municipal water, your water taps will keep flowing in the event of a power outage. But homes on well water aren’t so lucky—well pumps won’t work without electricity.

How will you cook if you lose electricity? If you have gas appliances, you should be able to light the pilot light with a match if you lose power. But if you have an electric stovetop and oven, you won’t be able to use your stove. You can, however, use a propane grill or an open fire to cook outdoors. If that’s your plan, refill the propane tank, or buy a cord of wood. And whatever your appliance situation, make sure you have a manual can opener.

Lowering the temperature of your refrigerator and freezer before the storm hits will help them stay cooler longer if the power goes out, thus increasing the likelihood that your food will be safe to eat after the power outage. Consider moving perishables like milk and meat into the freezer so they’ll stay colder. To conserve the cold air inside, avoid opening the refrigerator doors more than you absolutely have to.

If a winter power outage lasts more than a few days, you may run out of fresh food (or a means to prepare food). For this reason, it’s a good idea to keep plenty of nonperishable foods with long shelf lives like nut butters, canned fruit and juices, granola bars, and crackers on hand to keep yourself nourished.

Radios may seem a relic of the past, but these old-fashioned devices may just save your bacon if you lose power for an extended period. When modern methods of emergency alerts such as TVs and phones are offline, an emergency radio with fresh batteries may be your lifeline to news and information about dangerous conditions, even evacuation alerts. Better yet, select a radio can be charged in multiple ways. The Eton Odyssey radio, for example, can be charged via hand crank, USB-C, solar, and rechargeable and alkaline battery.

The Midland WR120B can be programmed to check weather in 25 local regions, so you can stay on top of loved ones’ forecasts Read the review.

Loss of power could be an excuse for a fun “campout” in the living room. Ahead of the storm, make sure your tent and sleeping bags are in good shape, or acquire these items if you don’t have them. Ensure you have plenty of heavy blankets, too. Then, when the power is out and temps in the house drop, set up the tent and unroll the sleeping bags. Body heat from people together in an enclosed space will help keep everyone warm. And you’ll have a fun story to tell!

If you’ve been meaning to caulk your windows, do it before cold weather strikes. Check the weatherstripping around your doors; odds are it’s seen better days. If your budget allows, replace or supplement your attic insulation. A less expensive way of sealing out some cold is to purchase some door draft stoppers, which you can tuck away in a closet until they are needed.

The worst time to buy a generator is the day you need one. If you live in an area that frequently loses power, consider purchasing a portable power station or a backup generator, which can be switched on manually or can automatically kick in when the power goes out. You can get generators powered by gasoline, natural gas, propane, or diesel (or even dual-fuel or inverter generators); solar generators are also an option but of course require a solar setup too.

After Testing 20 Air Purifiers, We Found One That Does Something the Rest Can’t

Your old potting mix isn't necessarily past its prime. Knowing when to refresh it – and which plants you can grow in it – will save money and reduce waste.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste. Don’t be too hasty. That mix could still have plenty of life left in it.

Over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away. Bulky materials, like peat moss and compost, break down over the summer, too. However, reusing potting soil is possible as long as the previous residents didn’t have diseases or serious pest infestations.

Some plants actually prefer leaner soil. Here, I describe six plants that are capable of thriving in old potting mix. I also provide some tips for refreshing the soil to give the new plants a little boost.

Nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is a beautiful flowering plant that grows as an annual in most gardens. Many types trail or vine, making them ideal for containers. The brilliant flowers come in shades of red, yellow, and orange, like in these Jewel Blend nasturtium seeds from Seed Needs on Amazon, which also offers other beautiful color mixes. Both the flowers and leaves are edible. If you live in USDA zone 9 or warmer, you can grow nasturtiums as perennials.

Nasturtiums are good candidates for recycled potting mix because they are unfussy, easy to grow, and generally thrive in poor soil. They are also easy to grow from seed. Sow seeds in your used potting mix next year when it’s warm enough. Place the container in a sunny spot and water when the top inch of soil dries.

Moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora) is another annual in most gardens. This low-growing succulent, native to South America, blooms in summer and fall with flowers that resemble small roses. You can find a lovely selection of moss rose seed varieties at Eden Brothers, with a choice of colors to brighten up your containers. Moss rose thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soil, making it ideal for containers. Plants need good drainage, so they can sometimes struggle in beds with heavy soil or poor drainage.

Grow your moss roses in reused potting mix enhanced with perlite, like this Riare organic perlite on Amazon, or something similar to boost drainage. Place them in a full-sun spot and let the soil dry out in between waterings. Avoid overfertilizing, which can lead to more leaves and fewer flowers.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Sedums (Sedum spp.) are reliable and popular perennials for garden beds, but they also grow well in containers. This is a large group of plants, many of which are succulents suited to dry, poor soil. Many gardeners love stonecrops like ‘Autumn Joy,’ which turn gorgeous shades of deep red in fall. You can buy Autumn Joy sedum from Nature Hills to enjoy its colorful late-season display. You can also choose from among low-growing and taller clump-forming sedums.

The most important part of refreshing old soil for growing sedum is to add a material, like perlite, to improve drainage. Place your pots in a sunny location and water only when the soil dries. Avoid using too much, if any, fertilizer.

Hens and chicks (Sempervivum spp.) are diminutive succulents that grow in rosettes and have delightfully fleshy leaves that can be bluish-green, copper, gold, reddish, or even two-toned. You can enjoy a mix of varieties with this hens and chicks plant collection from Hirt's Gardens Store on Amazon. While hens and chicks flower, they are grown mostly for their attractive foliage. Hardy perennials in many growing regions, hens and chicks also make great container plants. They produce small offsets, the chicks, that can be repotted for propagation.

Hens and chicks naturally grow in poor, rocky soil, so they should do well in your spent potting mix. Just be sure to add additional material to boost drainage. The best containers for hens and chicks are shallow and have adequate drainage holes, like this Deroma clay bowl planter from Target. Grow them in full sun or very light shade and water sparingly, letting the potting mix dry between waterings.

Calendula (Calendula officinalis), also known as pot marigold, is a short-lived perennial in zones 9 through 11, and an annual elsewhere. Though it is considered a flowering herb, many people grow calendula solely for its ornamental value. The flowers are daisy-like and usually bright orange or yellow, although they can also be red, white, or pink. You can pick up calendula seeds cheaply on Amazon, but Eden Brothers offers some gorgeous varieties, including the Pacific Beauty Mix and the Sunset Buff calendula pictured here.

A Mediterranean native, calendula appreciates warmth, sunlight, and well-draining soil. It won’t tolerate soggy soil. It can thrive in poor soil but benefits from a little refresh of old potting mix with compost. Water your potted calendula regularly, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Deadhead the flowers throughout the season to encourage additional blooms.

Like calendula, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) are mostly grown as annuals and are only hardy in zones 9 and higher. Cosmos are easy to grow from seed and reward you with feathery foliage and delicate flowers in shades of red, pink, white, yellow, and orange. Burpee sells a wide variety of cosmos seeds, including the beautiful ‘Sensation Mix’ pictured here. They make great cut flowers.

While cosmos tolerate poor soil, it’s best to refresh the old potting mix a little. Then, you can sow seeds and place the pot in a location with full sun. Use a large container, as cosmos can grow quite tall. Water the seeds and seedlings regularly to keep the soil moist, and then only sparingly.

While all of these, and many other plants, tolerate leaner soil, all plants will appreciate a little refresh of old, tired soil. A few simple steps will give you better results over the course of the growing season:

Remember that not all old soil should be used. Disease and pests can be passed on, so don’t take the risk. Also, if you’re growing plants that aren’t as tough as those listed here, it’s best to start over with fresh potting mix. You should also replace the mix if it has broken down so much that it becomes muddy and dense when wet.

Remember, old potting soil doesn’t necessarily belong in the trash. With a little refreshing and by choosing the right plants, you can recycle that old mix and use it for at least one more year.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

That veterinarians are humans too! I post a lot of information for other veterinary professionals, and I hope pet owners see the comments and realize how engaged the community is. âAnother Damn Rescueâ is a spicy shifter romcom where a veterinarian finds an injured âdogâ on the side of the road, only to realize heâs a wolf shifter. Fatigue! Thereâs compassion and ethical fatigue, where we feel helpless in the face of obstacles outside our reach. Some days I think, âI didnât help anyone today.â And thatâs not true; itâs the story we tell ourselves when weâre in that headspace.

Keep ALL of your records! Ask your vet to email you bloodworkand keep it in a folder. Take pictures of your pet's medications. Walking into the ER and saying âHereâs Fluffyâs last bloodworkâ and âhereâs the medication Fluffy is onâ is SO valuable!

XYLITOL!! It can cause fatal low blood sugar and liver damage. Itâs in sugar-free gum, and lately theyâve been calling it âbirch sugar,â so not a lot of people realize itâs the same thing.

Good mentorship is worth its weight in gold! Even the best veterinary school on the planet will not prepare you to step right into an ER without assistance. Ask for help, and find people who are willing to help you learn.

#7920. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! My Senior Cat Won’t Leave the Bedroom (November 16, 2026)

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every other Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

My cat, Mitzi, is 16 years and 8 months old. She has early-stage kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, which she is on medication for. About 2 months ago, she became deaf, and since then has refused to leave the master bedroom. I have moved her water bowl and litter box there and feed her there.

Is there anything I can do to get her to come out?â

At her age, sweet Mitzi has certainly earned the right to enjoy her golden years at her own pace, but I can imagine it is difficult to see her withdraw from the rest of the house, especially when you remember how she used to move around. However, I would not necessarily interpret her reluctance to leave the bedroom as something we need to correct. Losing her hearing can be quite disorienting. Imagine walking into a room where you can no longer hear footsteps, familiar voices, or the little sounds that help you understand what is happening around you. For Mitzi, the bedroom may now feel like her safest little world, where everything is familiar and predictable.

I actually think you have done a wonderful job adapting her environment by bringing her food, water, and litter box closer. Rather than encouraging her to leave right away, I would focus on helping her feel confident enough to explore if she wishes. You could start by sitting with her near the bedroom doorway, offering a favorite treat or a little affection. Gradually place treats a short distance beyond the door, allowing her to decide whether she wants to investigate.

Take care to only approach her within her visual field, avoid startling her while she sleeps, and keep pathways clear and nonslip. Think of it as extending her new world one comfortable step at a time, rather than asking her to return to her old routine.

There is one thing I would not overlook, though. Mitzi has both chronic kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, and at her age, reduced mobility or withdrawal can also be associated with arthritis, high blood pressure, visual changes, or inadequate control of her thyroid disease. I would recommend a senior cat veterinary checkup that includes blood pressure measurement, assessment for arthritis, and follow-up kidney and thyroid testing. Sometimes what looks like a behavioral change is actually a senior cat quietly telling us that they are in pain and something does not feel quite right.

Most importantly, please do not feel that you are encouraging a bad habit by keeping her essentials in the bedroom. You are adapting her home to meet her changing needs, and that is a beautiful expression of your love and care for her. If the bedroom is where Mitzi feels safe, eats well, drinks, uses her litter box, and enjoys your company, that can be a perfectly good quality of life.

At this stage, happiness is not measured by how much of the house she explores, but by how comfortable and secure she feels in the little world she chooses.

He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim currently lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.

#7919. The Best Dual-Fuel Generators for Home and Outdoor Use, Tested

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 16, 2026 7:25 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Dual-fuel generators offer the flexibility to run on either gasoline or propane, making them a versatile option for backup power. But with so many available, and many costing over $1,000, we tested a range of top models to help you find the right fit. Based on our results, we chose the Westinghouse WGen9500DF as our top pick for its powerful output, multiple starting options, and wide selection of outlets.

If you’re considering a dual-fuel generator but aren’t sure how much power you need or which features matter most, this guide can help. Below, we explain what to look for and share how five of the best dual-fuel generators performed in our hands-on tests.

Bottom line: Dual-fuel generators offer flexibility and power for home and outdoor use. Our tests highlight the best models to suit various needs and budgets.

Multifuel generators use gasoline or propane to provide electric power to your home, campground, or jobsite. But before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider whether it will meet your needs.

One key aspect of dual-fuel generators is you cannot run them indoors since they produce toxic fumes. Instead, you must set them up outside in a sheltered location and provide electrical power to appliances through an extension cord.

They are relatively heavy, weighing 100 to 200 pounds on average, and typically loud, sometimes exceeding the acceptable volumes allowed at RV parks. An inverter generator may be a better choice if you want a quiet generator. These generators have an enclosed body and supply power using a computer-controlled inverter instead of a noisier alternator.

However, if you need a decent amount of power, can see yourself regularly using more than one fuel type, and can handle a little extra weight and noise, a dual-fuel generator may be right for you.

The following dual-fuel generators represent the best the market has to offer in various categories. BobVila.com team members thoroughly tested each one, and we detail their pros and cons below.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 4.5/5

When it comes to choosing a good all-around generator, it’s tough to beat the Westinghouse WGen9500DF. This powerful generator runs on gasoline or propane, and selecting one or the other is as simple as flipping a switch. The WGen9500DF comes with a 6.6-gallon gasoline tank that will power the unit for up to 12 hours at a 25 percent load.

Actual runtime will depend on gasoline quality and how much power you’re drawing. On propane, it can run up to 7 hours on a 20-pound tank when drawing a 50 percent load. This model has a 120/240V-50A outlet, a 120/240V-30A locking outlet, and four 120V-20A GFCI outlets. At 9,500 running watts on gasoline, it’s powerful enough to run several tools simultaneously as well as an oven/range combo and clothes dryer separately.

The downsides? At 211 pounds, this is a heavy generator. It’s also loud, comparable to a motorcycle, which is enough to annoy neighbors yet reasonable for its output. If you’re looking for a quiet model to use during a power outage, this might not be it. It is, however, a powerhouse of electrical output using whichever fuel is preferred.

Read our full review: Westinghouse WGen9500DF Dual-Fuel Generator

What our tester says: “The remote-start key fob was my favorite feature—I could start the generator from a full 90 feet away once I put a fresh battery in the remote.” —Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Westinghouse dual-fuel generator at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 5/5; Power 4.5/5; Value 4.5/5

We tested the Pulsar 2200-watt inverter generator and found it great for powering small tools and devices for up to 8 hours. With a 1.18-gallon gas fuel tank, it supplies 1,800 running watts and 2,200 peak watts. With propane, it delivers 1,600 running watts and 2,000 peak watts.

Setup was a bit difficult initially due to a side panel we had to manually force off to access the oil fill port. After that, though, getting the generator ready to start for the first time took only a couple of minutes. After giving the recoil start a couple of pulls, we found that the engine came to life quickly. Our test rig included a couple of heat guns and hair dryers running simultaneously on different high and low settings to vary the load.

We found the generator handled 1,800 watts as advertised, but noise levels seemed louder than expected yet still in a reasonable range for output. Overall, this generator is a great option for light-duty needs such as small DIY projects and powering a couple of household appliances during an outage.

Get the Pulsar dual-fuel generator at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 5/5

This Champion 7,500-watt dual-fuel generator is powerful enough to supply critical home circuits during an electrical outage or enough electricity for an off-grid DIY building site. Its startup is easy and intuitive, with a manual choke lever, an electrical start switch, and a recoil cord. During testing, it started on the first pull every time. Using gas, the Champion generator produces 9,375 starting and 7,500 running watts. A full 7.7-gallon tank will provide up to 10 hours of runtime at a 50 percent electrical load. On propane, it operates at 8,400 starting and 6,750 running watts, working for up to 5.5 hours on a 20-pound propane tank. It has two GFCI-protected duplex household outlets, a 120V-30A locking outlet, and a 120/240V-30A locking outlet.

We used the Champion at a building site to run a portable table saw, miter saw, pancake air compressor, router, and several battery chargers. The tools ran perfectly, and the generator didn’t lag. At home, we used it to run heavy-duty extension cords to individual appliances, easily powering our fridge, deep freezer, microwave, and either a space heater or window air conditioner.

The only things we didn’t love about this generator were its fuel-guzzling nature and how difficult it was to transport. Its hard plastic wheels worked fine on pavement, but this 205-pound machine was not easy to roll across soft ground or lift into and out of our truck. For those looking to power an RV, be aware its 74 dB noise level will be too much for most campgrounds.

Get the Champion 7,500-watt dual-fuel generator at Blain’s Farm & Fleet.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 3/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 5/5; Power 4.5/5; Value 4/5

When it comes to portable generators, 12,000 watts is near the top end in terms of power. The DuroMax dual-fuel portable generator is a monster that can power several tools and appliances simultaneously without throwing a breaker. We tested the DuroMax using gasoline and propane. It can run up to 8 hours on a full 8.3-gallon gas tank when pulling a 50 percent load and up to 7 hours on propane at 50 percent capacity. It also has an electric starter and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that automatically shuts the generator down if it senses hazardous levels of CO gas.

The DuroMax comes with several plug-in ports that extend its usefulness. It has a 120V-30A outlet, a 120/240V-30A outlet, two 120V-20A outlets (for standard power cords), and one 120/240V-50A outlet. We tested it by running our refrigerator, most of the entertainment devices in our home, and even a window AC that pulls a lot of juice. It didn’t lag at all.

Though we liked its power, the DuroMax missed the mark in a few areas. It doesn’t have drop-down generator covers to protect the outlets, and it only has two 120V standard outlets. Like other gas-powered generators, it’s also loud. Overall, though, we found this generator powerful and easy to use, particularly at this price point.

Get the DuroMax dual-fuel generator at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 5/5

For a propane generator ready to go at a moment’s notice, the Wen DF11000T is a great option. This powerful generator produces 11,000 peak watts (required to start a powerful tool like a saw) and 8,300 running watts when using gasoline. It provides slightly less power when operating on propane–9,500 peak watts and 7,500 running watts–but that’s still a lot of electrical power.

After its initial break-in period, we rotated through several tests, using the Wen to power a chest freezer, full-size fridge-freezer, laptop, tankless water heater, shop lights, table, chop saw, and circ saw. It didn’t show signs of being under any load except for a split-second surge when we started up one of the saws (saws are notorious for drawing a lot of power on start-up). We tested all the tools and items we could think of and had no problems.

Then, we did it all again while running the Wen on propane. We got the same excellent results, and switching from gasoline to propane only required flipping a switch. This model comes with an electric start and has a large 6.6-gallon tank that will keep it running for up to 8.5 hours at a 50 percent load. It features four standard household outlets, a 30A outlet, and a 50A outlet.

Like many fuel-powered generators, the Wen is pretty loud, about as noisy as a lawn mower. Yet, based on our tests, that’s a small price to pay for the hefty amount of power this durable generator provides.

Get the Wen DF11000T dual-fuel generator at Amazon.

Before selecting several high-quality models for hands-on testing, we researched more than 24 dual-fuel generators, looking for quality construction, ease of use, portability, and power output. We gave some consideration to top manufacturers but didn’t automatically eliminate smaller or niche manufacturers if their generators were highly rated and competitively priced.

For actual testing, we assembled the generators and ran them according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We allotted time to models requiring break-in periods so the machines’ internal components could lubricate and settle before powering appliances or tools. Our team of testers then plugged in power tools, appliances, and more while using an online wattage calculator to estimate a suitable electrical load.

We awarded points to each model using a rubric considering ease of use, noise, portability, power, and value. The better a generator performed a test, the more points it received. After testing, we averaged the points to determine top performers.

To find the best dual-fuel generator for your home, campground, or worksite, consider the factors listed below, including fuel efficiency, fuel tank capacity, power output, and control panel configuration.

Dual-fuel generators have an isolated gasoline tank with a fuel capacity that ranges from as small as 2 gallons to more than 10 gallons. The larger the fuel tank on the generator, the longer the generator can provide gasoline-based power. But, as tank size increases, so does the size of the generator.

Fuel capacity does not affect how much propane you can use with your dual-fuel generator. Propane gas is stored under pressure in canisters, which attach to the generator with a hose and pressure regulator for direct fuel consumption.

The power output on dual-fuel generators is measured in watts. Manufacturers’ specs include peak power output and running power output. Peak power output refers to the maximum number of watts the generator can provide at any one time. Running power output equals the average number of watts produced during use.

Dual-fuel generators generally produce a power output from 1,000 watts to over 12,000 watts, depending on their size. Gasoline produces a higher wattage than propane, so many manufacturers of dual-fuel technology break wattage into propane peak and running outputs and gasoline peak and running outputs.

For greater power output needs, users may need to consider a standby generator rather than a portable dual-fuel option.

You can start your dual-fuel generator with an electric start switch or a recoil cord.

A generator’s operating noise level is measured in decibels. To understand the range of sound produced by a generator, consider these common sounds and their equivalent operating dB level:

Many dual-fuel generators produce 50 to 90 dB of noise, depending on fuel type (gasoline runs louder than propane) and power output. The most common range is between 65 dB and 75 dB, comparable to the sound of normal conversation.

The quietest dual-fuel generators combine dual-fuel technology and inverter technology to create a dual-fuel inverter generator.

Dual-fuel generators are typically large and heavy, with hoses or tanks that make them difficult to carry and move. Thus, some manufacturers include wheel kits for tilting the generator back and rolling it to the desired location.

You may also be able to purchase a wheel kit separately to add to your existing generator or replace an older wheel kit that doesn’t work well anymore. Either way, a wheel kit makes transporting a portable dual-fuel generator much easier.

Lift hook bars are handy on jobsites, allowing workers to attach the generator to a hook-and-pulley system and raise or lower it instead of carrying it up or down stairs or ladders. In industrial settings, this feature helps raise the generator onto a walkway or platform.

A lift hook bar will increase the generator’s weight (and likely the price), so don’t look for a generator with this feature unless you truly plan to use it.

Most dual-fuel generators are between 22 inches long by 22 inches wide by 22 inches high and 35 inches long by 30 inches wide by 30 inches high. They typically weigh between 100 and 250 pounds.

If you plan to move the generator frequently, figure size and weight prominently into your decision. Make sure the model you choose fits into your vehicle so you can transport it as needed. Remember, however, that larger, heavier motors are also the most powerful. You’ll want to find the right balance of size, weight, and power to meet your needs.

Gasoline and propane each have their pros and cons as fuel options. Gasoline is easier to find, but propane costs less. Propane is a better fuel source in hot summer weather, while gas burns better in the cold. A dual-fuel generator lets you choose one or the other based on immediate circumstances.

Using both fuel sources, one after the other, greatly increases a generator’s runtime. Users can run to the gas station to refuel while the generator keeps providing power on propane.

Before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider the answers to the following frequently asked questions.

A dual-fuel generator operates like a single-fuel generator, except it can burn propane and gasoline to produce electrical energy. It converts mechanical energy produced by the burning fuels to force the movement of electrical charges and generate electricity.

While some single-fuel generators can be adapted for use with natural gas, this isn’t the case with dual-fuel generators. Unless specially designed, dual-fuel generators do not run on natural gas and cannot be adapted for this purpose.

Propane gas is less expensive than gasoline, nearly impossible to spill, and burns cleaner, resulting in less wear on the engine over time. Running a dual-fuel generator on propane will save money but slightly decrease the machine’s peak and running watts.

Runtime is determined by fuel efficiency and fuel tank capacity. On average, a standard dual-fuel generator runs about 8 to 10 hours on propane.

If power is the goal, then the DuroMax dual-fuel generator is one of the best options to help ensure the campsite or essential home appliances have power for hours.

Depending on how much wattage a home draws under normal situations, attaching a high-capacity dual-fuel generator to its electrical system may be possible, but it’s not a DIY project.An electrician must install a transfer switch connecting the generator to the home’s electrical main. When the power goes out, the transfer switch automatically switches the incoming power from the grid to the generator. In most cases, the generator will be classified as a “standby generator” because it’s always ready to start generating electricity. Most portable generators are too small to run an entire home.

Generators running on gasoline are typically louder than those running on propane since burning propane requires less energy.

As with most outdoor tools and large household appliances, you will want to take dual-fuel generators to a local recycling plant for recycling.

Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!

Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval! And, somewhat gloriously, SJP's approach to festive decor has the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, which means you don't need a celebrity-sized budget to recreate the look. In fact, all you really need is baby's breath.

This underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets. But when Kristin Davis posted an Instagram video of herself arranging flowers blindfolded (as one does), Sarah Jessica Parker left a surprising comment: “You can use babies breath in your Christmas tree.” Say what?

Now, Kristin Davis (who worked at a florist in college) wasn’t keen on using it for her own tree (very Charlotte-coded), but she did share a rule worth stealing: if you're going to do it, then always arrange flowers in odd numbers, like three or five.

For me, though, SJP’s comment about using baby’s breath in her Christmas tree has set my imagination alight! And with that in mind, I asked some experts how I could use them in my own holiday decoration this year.

The biggest risk when it comes to stealing Sarah Jessica Parker's idea is overdoing it. Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, says, “The main mistake is using too much. The beauty of baby’s breath is its lightness.” Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home puts it even better, saying, “One loose spiral is elegant. Three is a snowstorm, and the tree disappears behind it.”

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Remember that odd-number rule? CEO of Florals Memories Nadi Melam clips her baby’s breath into “clouds” and adds them in threes, noting, “Baby’s breath looks beautiful on trees because of negative space.” Translation: let the tree breathe!

For a spiral, Brooks gathers five to seven stems, wires each bunch at the base, and tucks the ends deep into the branches. Sabbatini also skips pushing loose stems into the tree and instead secures each little bundle with florist wire or ribbon.

Fresh baby’s breath is a diva out of water. Brooks says fresh stems “wilt within a day or two indoors,” while dried versions keep their shape all season and can be packed away for next year. Melam agrees that dried is “far easier to work with.” If you do love fresh, just be sure to add it on Christmas Eve.

If you don't have time for the drying process, this Bexikou dried baby’s breath bouquet comes ready to use, and its short white stems are well suited to wiring into small, airy clusters for your tree.

Drying your own for a Sarah Jessica Parker-style tree is simple. Bundle five to seven stems with twine, hang them upside down in a dark, warm, well-ventilated room, and check after five days, as outlined in our guide to growing baby’s breath. If you’re short on time, ready-dried bunches work just as well.

On an artificial tree, Brooks adds fine floral wire around the branch wire, since the stems are too light to stay put when someone brushes past.

Warm white lights, clear glass ornaments, and velvet ribbon are baby’s breath’s best friends. Brooks adds pearl baubles and silver or soft gold ribbon to the list, but warns that rustic burlap and heavy red ornaments “fight it.” Treat baby’s breath as one of just two or three ideas on the tree, not the whole script.

Pair your baby’s breath with a strand of Northlight 100-count warm white LED mini lights, which stay cool to the touch and give the soft, candlelit glow that suits a delicate white filler.

Dried stems are brittle and, as Melam notes, highly flammable. Use cool LED lights and keep bunches away from hot bulbs and open flames. Baby’s breath is also mildly toxic to cats, so if pets are around, keep it to the upper two-thirds of the tree and sweep up anything that falls.

Baby’s breath is easy to grow, so sow seeds next spring, cut and dry the blooms in summer, and next December’s tree is sorted. Will your tree look like a Manhattan brownstone from a certain Sarah Jessica Parker-fronted TV series? Possibly, but only if you resist the urge to add a fourth bunch.

#7916. Three Cats, One Rabies Outbreak: What Happens Next?

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Every time the topic of vaccines comes up, thereâs always someone who questions whether our pets really need them. Asking questions about medical care is perfectly reasonable (in fact, informed pet parents should!), but dismissing vaccination without understanding the risks is another story.

Rabies is a perfect example. This is not some historical disease or something that only affects animals in remote areas or underdeveloped countries. It can infect mammals, including our own cats, dogs, and even us. Whatâs even scarier is that once the clinical signs appear, rabies is almost always fatal, making prevention essential.

Recent events in Quebec offer a timely reminder. Amid an emerging wildlife outbreak, three domestic cats tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies in 2026. Although these numbers pale in comparison to the number of infected wildlife recorded since December 20241, it demonstrates how a disease circulating in wild animals can reach our pets.

And this isn't just a Canadian concern. Rabies variants and wildlife risks differ by region, but keeping pets appropriately vaccinated is a responsibility shared by pet parents everywhere.

Despite its name, raccoon-strain rabies isn't exclusive to raccoons; they are simply the reservoir species of this particular variant of the rabies virus. Skunks and other mammals â including cats â can also become infected.

Rabies attacks the central nervous system. It spreads mainly through the bite of an infected animal, when virus-containing saliva enters the body. Saliva can also transmit the virus if it reaches an open wound, the eyes, nose, or mouth.

Raccoon rabies had been eliminated in Quebec following an outbreak between 2006 and 2009, but the virus resurfaced in 2024. Since then, more outbreaks have appeared, and case numbers have climbed sharply in 2026, particularly in MontÃ©rÃ©gie. By October 29, 328 animals had tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies across the province. The three infected cats are examples of how a virus circulating in wildlife can also reach our pets, even though cats are not the main reservoir responsible for spreading this variant.

Cats are naturally curious, territorial predators. They investigate unfamiliar scents, watch moving animals, explore hidden spaces, and sometimes pursue creatures that would be better left alone. These behaviors are normal expressions of feline biology, not evidence that a cat is being reckless.

Unfortunately, wildlife encounters can turn dangerous very quickly. A raccoon searching for food near a house may cross paths with an outdoor cat. A skunk hiding beneath a shed may be investigated by a curious feline. Even a sick or disoriented wild animal can catch a cat's attention, and one of the hallmarks of rabies infection in wild animals is a reduced fear of humans and predators as the infection attacks the nervous system. And cats being cats, curiosity can get them into trouble! These encounters don't just happen deep in the woods. A backyard, garage, or garden fence can be enough.

One of the infected cats was believed to have contracted rabies after contact with a wild animal. Another case led to three people receiving preventive treatment following possible exposure.

Rabies doesn't always turn an animal into a movie villain, either. Early signs can be subtle, which is why recognizing unusual behavior and reporting possible exposure is so important.

When people think of rabies, they often picture a snarling animal, dripping saliva, and attacking everything in sight. Hollywood certainly loves that version! Unfortunately, rabies doesn't always come with such obvious special effects.

In cats, the first signs can be surprisingly subtle. A normally friendly kitty may suddenly become grumpy, hide more than usual, vocalize differently, lose interest in food, or behave in ways that seem completely out of character. Since cats are already experts at keeping their humans guessing, a sudden behavior change can sometimes be easy to dismiss. But when a cat starts acting noticeably different from their usual, wonderfully weird self, it's worth paying attention.

As the disease progresses, neurological signs become more apparent. Affected cats may become disoriented, walk unsteadily, have difficulty swallowing, drool excessively, develop weakness, or eventually become paralyzed. Some become unusually aggressive or sensitive to touch, sounds, and light.

There is also a less dramatic presentation called paralytic rabies, sometimes referred to as âdumb rabiesâ. Instead of becoming aggressive, affected animals may become unusually quiet, weak, or withdrawn. Difficulty swallowing, a drooping jaw, and progressive paralysis can follow. So no, a rabid animal doesn't necessarily look like it's auditioning for a horror movie.

Of course, these signs can also occur with other neurological conditions, injuries, and intoxications. Nobody should attempt to diagnose rabies based on behavior alone. A cat showing sudden, unexplained neurological changes needs prompt veterinary attention, particularly if wildlife exposure is possible.

Here's another catch: rabies can take weeks, sometimes even months, to show itself. A cat may seem perfectly fine after an encounter with an infected animal, but that doesn't mean the virus isn't already in its body. So if a possible exposure happens, don't wait for your cat to look sick before calling the vet. By then, it may be too late.

Sadly, once rabies reaches the clinical stage, there is no cure, and the outcome is almost always fatal. That's why a suspected exposure should never be a wait-and-see situation. Don't wait for signs to appear; contact your veterinarian right away. With rabies, prevention isn't just better than treatment; it's our best chance to protect our cats in the first place.

Think your indoor cat doesn't need a rabies vaccine? Think again! Indoor cats have fewer opportunities to encounter wildlife, but escapes happen, doors get left open, and sometimes wildlife finds its way indoors. Nobody plans these little adventures, least of all the cat!

Rabies vaccination is also required by law for cats in many countries and jurisdictions. Even where it isn't mandatory, keeping your cat vaccinated is an important part of preventive care. Ask your veterinarian about the appropriate schedule for your cat.

And remember, vaccination doesn't mean ignoring a possible exposure. If your vaccinated cat is bitten by a potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian right away.

If your cat is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, contact your veterinarian immediately, even if your cat seems perfectly fine. Bite wounds can hide beneath all that lovely fur, and waiting for signs to appear is not an option.

Keep your cat away from other animals and don't try to catch or handle the wild animal. Report suspicious wildlife to local authorities and let trained professionals deal with it.

If a person is bitten or scratched, or infected saliva enters an open wound or contacts the eyes, nose, or mouth, wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Post-exposure treatment can prevent rabies from developing, so don't delay.

And please, leave dead wildlife alone. No bare-handed investigations or impromptu rescue missions!

Quebec is also fighting the outbreak through wildlife surveillance and vaccination campaigns using vaccine baits. These efforts help protect wild animals and reduce further spread.

Cats will be cats. A rustling bush can become the most fascinating thing in the universe, and a passing raccoon may look like an invitation to investigate. We can't blame them for being curious. We can give them safer ways to enjoy their adventures.

We all know the key to a happy and healthy canine relationship is training, and the key to training often lies in rewarding good behavior. The trouble with this equation is that, for many dogs, positive reinforcement needs to come in the form of a high-value treat, which usually means high calories.

You might have tried switching to healthier options like carrot slices or using pieces of their usual kibble, but letâs face it: the really tasty treats are what keep our dogs motivated, and thereâs no such thing as a really tasty, really healthy dog treatâ¦ Right?

Thatâs what I thought until I was introduced to Fiber Veggie Bites from Choolip.

These bite-sized chewy treats made from garden-harvested ingredients are proof that high-value dog treats donât have to be unhealthy.

One thing dog trainers, behaviorists, and veterinary professionals generally agree on is that positive reinforcement is the best and most effective way to train our dogs. Simple commands like âsitâ or âcomeâ are pretty easy to master, but the more we ask of our dogs, the greater the reward needs to be.

Calling my dog in from the backyard is one thing, but teaching him to ignore distractions on a crowded beach or a forest filled with sounds, scents, and squirrels presents a much greater challenge. I need him to know that turning away from the excitement is worth it, and that usually means dialing up the praise and rewarding him with a really tasty treat. Of course, the really high-value treats tend to be greasy and smelly, or over-processed and high in calories. Before you know it, youâve blown through your dogâs daily calorie allowance, and itâs almost guaranteed that cleaning up tomorrowâs bowel movements will need a hose and bucket rather than a trusty poop bag!

Then thereâs the guilt. You want to treat your best buddy to their favorite snacks, but you also want to give them the healthiest foods available.

Some owners â myself included â are fortunate enough to have a dog that is as excited by a piece of carrot as they are by a milk bone, so itâs easy to deliver healthy treats daily.

#7913. The Best Outdoor Christmas Lights of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

What would the holidays be without outdoor Christmas lights to illuminate the winter darkness? Whether you’re shopping for tiny twinkle lights or a string of large bulbs that create a nostalgic look, the 10 tested options on our list of top picks are sure to add a festive feeling to your home.

Since sets of lights can cost as little as $5 or over $100, it can be challenging to know which are worth the price and effort to hang. That’s why we used these strings, nets, and projectors for a full 2 weeks, subjecting them to freezing rain and snow, falls on concrete, and overnight illumination sessions. Based on our tests, we chose the Prextex Christmas Clear White Wire 100 Light Set as the best overall option for its ease of use, durability, and attractive bright white light.

When selecting the set that’s right for you, consider the lights’ string length, color, and control features. Imagine how they’ll pair with the overall look you’re creating for upcoming holiday celebrations as well as the skills and techniques required to install them. Once you’ve checked out each set, be sure to scan the shopping tips at the end of this guide before choosing the best outdoor Christmas lights for your space.

Bottom line: Find the perfect outdoor Christmas lights for your home with our tested and reviewed top picks, offering options for every budget and style.

The best outdoor Christmas lights include sets that consistently provide bright, clear light and last for a reasonable amount of time. There are a variety of styles on this list to fit different tastes, architecture, and themes. Remember—no matter the style, the best lights are the ones that make you feel like the holidays have finally arrived.

Our Ratings: Setup 4.5/5; Appearance 4.8/5; Durability 5/5; Storage 4.5/5; Value 4.8/5

It’s not easy to choose one set of lights as the “best.” But since these Prextex Christmas lights are so versatile, attractive, and durable, we think almost everyone would agree they’re worth their relatively low price. These small twinkle lights come on a 20-foot-long string with a 13-inch lead wire and a 5-foot end connector. They’re designed for indoor and outdoor use and are sized so as to not look out of place in either location.

We wrapped these white wire lights up a wooden porch beam for our tests. They held up without issue against rain, snow, freezing temperatures, and plenty of bumps from two rowdy dogs. Should a bulb get broken, however, the package includes two extras as well as two replacement fuses. It also comes with two flasher bulbs, which you’ll need to swap out with two regular ones if you want your lights to twinkle. While that’s not ideal, we actually prefer solid lights in that spot anyway, so we weren’t too upset. The other potential downside of this set is that bulbs are incandescent rather than LED, so they may not last as long—though the manufacturer promises up to 2,200 hours of use.

What our tester says: “We love having these lights on our deck so much that I doubt we’ll take them down once the holidays are over. Their white light is bright enough to add visibility to our table, and they create a cozy feel that we think will be appropriate year-round.”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Our Ratings: Setup 4.5/5; Appearance 4.5/5; Durability 4.8/5; Storage 4/5; Value 5/5

The BHCLight extra-long Christmas lights illuminate the holidays at a foot-by-foot price that’s hard to beat. Each 95-foot string contains 240 LED warm-white lights—more than sufficient to add a cozy glow. If that’s not the color you’re after, they come in eight other options, including red, green, bright white, blue, and color changing. They’re approved for indoor and outdoor use (they’re waterproof), so they offer versatility along with holiday cheer.

Easy to control via a button located near the electrical plug, these lights display in eight modes: combination, waves, sequential, slow glow, chasing, slow fade, twinkle, and steady on. This string’s shortcomings are that it’s on the thinner side, and it cannot be plugged into another string to create a longer set of lights. Still, we had more than enough length to encircle a large bush in our yard, and its light weight made it easy to drape.

What our tester says: “We like to decorate for the holidays, but we’re also busy, so we tend to want to cover a lot of space quickly. Like many options on this list, they also come in red, green, blue, multicolor, and several other colors.

One of the best things about this pick is its lightweight but strong and flexible cord, which was easy to wrap around objects and extend across our mantle, on top of cabinets, and along the roofline. Though we eventually ended up using these inside, they are definitely bright and durable enough for outdoor use. While these lights are rated for both indoor and outdoor use, their stiff cord makes them a bit better for outside—as we found it a bit too thick for stringing on our tree and mantle. Outdoors, that thickness made it easy to install them in nice, straight rows. Back inside for storage, however, we once again found the thickness challenging because getting them to compress down into a compact size wasn’t easy.

To us, the most important factors for choosing outdoor Christmas lights decorations are attractiveness and durability, so that’s what we focused on most in our tests. After unboxing each set of lights, we got right to work hanging them up. We ran strings along our roof, across the fence, and around bushes and poles. We took note of how easy they were to hang and whether we had to be careful to keep any components out of the elements. After a couple of weeks of wet winter weather, we undid all our work by taking the lights down, dropping them on cement to see if any bulbs would break, and packing them up to determine if their original packaging still provided enough space for storage.

Outdoor lights come in a surprising variety of shapes, sizes, and colors. Smart LED Christmas lights, for example, can emit hundreds, if not thousands, of colors from a single bulb. Also, different bulbs of different sizes create different looks and require different choices regarding Christmas light storage. Keep your decor style and preferences in mind while selecting between outdoor Christmas lighting ideas.

The most common outdoor Christmas light styles include:

There are also outdoor Christmas light projectors, which aren’t Christmas lights in a traditional sense, but they can add a festive flair to a holiday display.

Outdoor Christmas lights come in various lengths, from 10 feet to 100 feet or more. Measure the distance the lights will need to cover to get an idea of the right number of strings for the lighting design, accounting for any swag or draping for effect. Falling a few feet short can easily impact your outdoor Christmas display.

If you’re considering an outdoor Christmas light projector, remember the area the display can cover is explicitly defined in terms of square footage. While you can move the projector farther from the house to expand the display size, that may affect the quality of the images and the density of the colors it displays.

Electricity and solar are the main power sources for outdoor Christmas lights, though you can also sometimes find battery-operated Christmas lights. Of the two, electricity is by far the more reliable. Electricity provides consistent power, though it also requires extension cords and access to an outdoor outlet in the right location.

Solar-powered Christmas lights are less common but are still a viable option. They’re an energy saver, generating energy via a solar panel during the day, but they aren’t without their flaws. The biggest problem is power consistency. Solar power must be stored to keep the lights running after the sun goes down. Many of these lights shine brightly for about 1 or 2 hours but then dim as power fades. Yes, they save power, but they’re not nearly as bright or consistent as electric lights.

LED Christmas light bulbs use light-emitting diodes instead of filaments like incandescent bulbs. The diodes require less energy and last longer than filaments, creating a long-lasting, energy-efficient light bulb. LED lights also remain cool to the touch, reducing the risk of fire. Outdoor LED Christmas lights come in a wider variety of colors than incandescent ones. When paired with smart features, they can create a rainbow of options.

The best Christmas lights can include extra features like:

Even if you’ve been helping with outdoor Christmas lights since you were a kid, you might still have a few questions about this particular category of string lights. Our answers to the following frequently asked questions can help you get your lights selected and installed so that your home looks its best this holiday season.

When hanging outdoor Christmas lights, recruit a helper, get a sturdy ladder, and prepare for at least a few hours of work. Start with a string near an electrical outlet and hang your Christmas lights by following the roofline. Have your helper hold the ladder for stability. If the lights you’re hanging don’t have clips, you can attach them with nails, a staple gun, or removable light clips. Of these options, the removable clips are easiest and cause the least damage to the home.

Unlike indoor Christmas lights, outdoor Christmas lights should be 100 percent waterproof. If they’re not, they could short out the first time it rains or snows. Check the IP rating, which consists of two digits. The first number indicates dust and debris resistance, and the second indicates water resistance on a scale of 0 to 9. Waterproof outdoor Christmas lights should have a rating of at least 4 (in the second digit) or higher. Lights with a 4 or 5 can resist light rain, though they may not do well in extremely wet weather.

Yes, Christmas outdoor lights are safe to leave on all night. However, you might want to connect them to a timer to save energy.

Yes, LED outdoor Christmas lights last longer than older-style bulbs. The U.S. Department of Energy says that LED bulbs last up to 25 times longer than incandescent bulbs.

The size of bulbs you choose for your outdoor Christmas lights depends mostly on your personal preferences. In our tests, we really liked the look of Noma’s C9 Christmas Lights on our roofline and mini lights like the Prextex White Wire Lights wrapped around our covered porch’s beams.

Some outdoor lighting will have a control box near its plug that isn’t waterproof and must be covered or otherwise kept out of the elements. Other options for outdoor Christmas lights will be fully waterproof, as stated on the packaging.

Choosing the best color for outdoor Christmas lights is 100 percent personal preference, so pick whichever color or colors you prefer! If you’re looking to change colors this year and want to responsibly part ways with old lights, see our guide on recycling Christmas lights for more information.

Like color and size, brightness for outdoor Christmas lights mostly comes down to personal preference. Cool white lights may be best for you if you prefer something on the brighter end of the spectrum. Colored or warm white options typically aren’t quite as bright.

Though she forgot to check each bulb before installation, the quality offered by today’s lights ensured she created that house-on-fire look her own Aunt Bethany loves.

Wouldn't it be magical to spot an owl in your backyard? You might be surprised how much difference the right plants can make...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's something rather magical about spotting an owl in your backyard. These mysterious nighttime visitors can be surprisingly elusive, but there are ways to make your garden a more welcoming place for them. And no, you don't need acres of woodland or a sprawling country estate to get your very own owl hangout started.

The secret is to think beyond the owls themselves (although there's never any harm in making an owl nest box) and create a garden that supports the wildlife they depend on.

Whether you want to lure in your birth month owl, or find yourself – much like Justin Bieber – welcoming in any owl that flits by, there are plenty of ways to make your backyard more appealing to these beautiful birds of prey. And the good news? Well, you can make a surprisingly big difference with just five plants.

That's right, folks! If you want more owls in your garden, that means providing shelter for small mammals, encouraging insects and other prey, and offering trees and shrubs where owls can perch, roost or potentially nest.

From tall native grasses to berry-producing shrubs and evergreen trees, then, these are some of the best additions for creating an owl-friendly backyard.

Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a fantastic native grass for an owl-friendly garden, particularly if you have a sunny spot where you can let it grow relatively undisturbed.

Why? Well, because its tall stems and dense clumps provide valuable cover for small mammals, including voles and mice, which are important prey for many owl species. The grass also offers shelter for other wildlife through winter, when more exposed parts of the garden can become less hospitable.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Switchgrass is particularly useful in meadow-style plantings, where it can grow alongside native wildflowers. It produces attractive seedheads in late summer and fall, too, and it's a relatively low-maintenance perennial once established.

Give it a sunny position and well-drained soil, then, and leave some of its growth standing over winter rather than cutting everything back in fall. You may just find it swiftly becomes your new favorite garden plant, let alone the best part of your owl hangout!

If you want to make your garden more appealing to owls, don't underestimate the value of evergreen trees! Native pines and spruces provide year-round cover, with dense branches offering potential daytime roosting spots and sheltered perches. Their evergreen foliage can also make wildlife feel more protected from disturbance and exposure.

Different owl species have different preferences, but trees are an important part of the habitat for many woodland-dwellers like barred owls. Some species also use natural cavities in mature trees for nesting.

If you have room, consider something like this stunning Eastern White Pine from Nature Hills. Just remember that a newly planted sapling is unlikely to become an instant owl retreat, though, so it's always better to preserve mature trees where you can!

A slightly wild patch of blackberry brambles (Rubus spp.) might not be everyone's idea of a perfectly manicured garden, but it's a genius addition to anyone hoping to turn their yard into an owl hangout. After all, blackberry thickets provide dense cover for small critters and nesting birds, not to mention food and shelter for plenty others besides.

Why does this matter for owls? Because a garden that supports a healthy range of small animals can help provide the prey that visiting owls need, of course! And you don't have to let blackberries take over your entire yard, either. A small patch of something like Baby Cakes® Blackberry Bush from Nature Hills along a boundary or at the back of a wildlife-friendly border can provide plenty of habitat value.

Just remember that brambles can spread, so give them room and keep growth away from paths and areas where people regularly walk.

Serviceberry (Amelanchier spp.) is a beautiful native shrub or small tree that brings several seasons of wildlife interest to the garden; think white flowers that attract pollinators, followed by edible berries in summer, which are enjoyed by birds and other wildlife.

Its value doesn't stop with the berries; serviceberry also supports insects and provides useful woody cover, helping to create a more diverse backyard habitat. For an owl-friendly garden, this is all about supporting the wider food web... but hey, it helps that it's a stunner, too!

Goldenrod (Solidago spp.) is often overlooked as a wildlife plant, but its bright yellow flowers provide an important late-season source of nectar and pollen for bees, butterflies and other insects. Those insects, in turn, help support other wildlife, including small birds and mammals.

Some smaller owl species also eat large insects, making insect-rich habitats like goldenrod a must for your owl hangout! Especially as it's a lovely way to add late-summer and fall color to your garden. Many varieties are native to North America, and once established, they're generally easy to grow.

Something like the Fireworks Solidago (Goldenrod) Plant from Burpee is a great way to go!

These five plants are a great starting point for your owl hangout, but there are plenty of other native choices that can help make your backyard more wildlife-friendly. #

Viburnums, for example, produce berries that feed birds and other wildlife, while their dense branching offers useful cover, too. Native dogwoods offer flowers, berries and dense branching that can provide shelter for wildlife, not to mention some much-added beauty to any yard (there's a reason they're swiftly replacing magnolias for a lot of people!).

Junipers offer dense year-round cover and provide berry-like cones that are eaten by birds and small mammals. And purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea) attract pollinators and produce seedheads that feed birds and other critters, too.

Of course, planting is a brilliant starting point, but there are a few other things you can do to make your garden more appealing to these fascinating birds. As ever, try leaving some areas of longer grass and natural vegetation rather than tidying every corner. Keep mature trees where possible, particularly those with natural cavities, and consider whether a species-appropriate owl nest box might be suitable for your local area.

It's also important to avoid rodent poisons, as owls can be exposed to rodenticides when they eat poisoned mice and rats. Keep lights to a minimum after the sun goes down, as they can confuse nocturnal birds and critters. And, finally, remember that owls need peace and quiet; take care to avoid disturbing potential roosting and nesting areas, particularly during breeding season.

You might not spot an owl straight away, but by planting for wildlife and allowing your garden to become a little more natural, you'll be creating a much richer habitat for all sorts of visitors. And who knows? Before too long, your owl hangout might just be the most buzzing nightspot in town...

As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#7911. The Most Common Fatal Diseases in Cats, and How to Avoid Them

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way. But considering many serious feline health conditions respond well to early intervention, a little knowledge can go a long way. Here are eight of the most serious, what they tend to look like, and practical steps that can help lower the risk. The aim isnât to worry anyone, just to help owners feel prepared.

Heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam. The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Vets rely on heart scans, chest X-rays, and blood tests to discover heart disease.

Lowering the risk: Genetics play a big part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

Kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which shows up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

Lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

Lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

This is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight quickly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

Up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

Lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

Rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

Lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

Lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

Spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

Lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

Not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a plan for each cat.
