#7893. Spring Returns to Ezequiel’s Cottage Garden in Argentina

While many of our gardens are settling in for winter, Ezeiza, Argentina, is enjoying the last stretch of spring before summer arrives in December. Today we’re heading back to visit Ezequiel. We’ve followed his cottage garden through the seasons over the years, including another beautiful spring visit. After some difficult weather, he is back with another update as his garden fills with flowers ahead of summer.

I hope you are all doing very well during the autumn in the North. In my country, following the harsh and troublesome “El Niño” weather phenomenon, the long-awaited and much-loved spring has finally arrived in my cottage garden in Ezeiza.

Plants and flowers are just beginning to emerge, a promise of the summer that will be in full swing by December here in the Southern Hemisphere. Penstemons, salvias, irises, verbenas, dahlias, bulbines, daisies, and my lemon tree… Everything has begun to stir, grow, and grace us with beautiful blossoms, lovely scents, and fragrances.

Thank you, as always, for being there! And thank you for sharing in the joy of my garden.

From Argentina, sending you my best regards and a big hug.

A look into Ezequiel’s cottage garden in Ezeiza, Argentina.

‘Hot Lips’ salvia (Salvia microphylla ‘Hot Lips’, Zones 7–10) in bloom.

Louisiana iris (Iris × louisiana, Zones 4–9) showing off.

Purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea, Zones 3–9) are flowering next to the large sweep of lavender (Lavandula cvs., Zones 5–10) along the side of the driveway. I can practically smell the lavender looking at this photo!

This massive lantana (Lantana camara, Zones 8–11) stopped me in my tracks! Here in the North, we usually grow lantana as an annual because it isn’t winter hardy. Seeing what this tender perennial can become in a warmer climate is pretty incredible.

Bearded iris (Iris cvs., Zones 3–9), California poppy (Eschscholzia californica, Zones 8–10), and orange bulbine (Bulbine frutescens, Zones 9–11) make a colorful combination in this perennial bed.

Another view of the massive lantana, this time with a gorgeous specimen crimson bottlebrush (Callistemon citrinus, Zones 8–11) in full bloom.

Another view of the backyard. This photo has me wondering just how far it extends. I’m so curious about the layout of this garden—it seems like there’s something new to discover just about everywhere!

Thank you for bringing us back to your beautiful garden, Ezequiel! It’s always such a treat to see what’s growing in your corner of the world, especially while our seasons here in the North are moving in the opposite direction.

Why wait until spring? Planting fruit trees before winter gives the a chance to establish their roots before the growing season gets underway.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In France, gardeners and farmers have a saying that November 25 – the day Saint Catherine is celebrated – is the ideal day to plant a tree. ("À la Sainte-Catherine, tout bois prend racine.”) That may not apply literally to every tree species, but I can tell you this much: November is an excellent time to plant many kinds of fruit trees as long as the ground is not frozen.

Growing fruit trees is a gift to yourself that keeps on giving. Each tree in your home orchard can provide delicious homegrown harvests for years to come. Planting fruit trees in November offers many benefits. The cooler late-fall weather reduces transplanting stress, and seasonal rains keep the soil moist. That helps the trees establish roots before spring growth begins.

Which fruit trees should top your list? Many wonderful fruit trees are great to plant in November, so choose the one that grows your favorite fruit. But be sure to consider your local climate. Each fruit tree species has its own hardiness zone that indicates its cold tolerance. Some – like apples and pears – also have winter chilling requirements. You’ll also want to consider the mature size of the tree and be certain it will fit into your landscape.

Does life get any better than wandering out to the backyard and pulling a crisp apple right off your own tree and taking a bite? So when you consider planting a tree in November, don’t overlook apples. Apple trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–8, depending on the variety. You can plant either a bare-root apple tree or a container-grown tree in November, as long as the soil is not frozen, although spring planting is often safer in colder zones 3–4.

There are many apple varieties to choose from. Most won’t fruit reliably on their own, so check their pollination requirements when you purchase your tree. Your tree may require a compatible cross-pollinator that flowers at the same time. For a great pairing, try a ‘Honeycrisp’ apple tree alongside a ‘Gala’ apple tree – both available from Trees.com – which can cross-pollinate and give you two delicious varieties to harvest. If you only have room for one tree, ‘Golden Delicious’ is partially self-fertile and can produce fruit without a partner, although you'll generally get a better crop with cross-pollination.

Plant your apple tree in a full sun location in well-draining soil. You may want to stake the tree to prevent any windrock until its roots anchor it well. You can buy a tree-staking kit from Amazon, but if your area is very windy, a crossbar attached to two posts will provide more support.

Pears feel like a fancier fruit than apples, but the trees are just as easy to grow and maintain. Like pear slices in your salad? With your own pear tree, you can pick sweet fruit anytime during the harvest season. Pear trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–10, depending on the variety.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Like apple trees, pear trees grow best in a full sun location in well-draining soil. As with most apple trees, pear trees are not usually self-pollinating. That means that you will need two compatible cultivars for reliable pollination and fruit set. However, there are exceptions. Both the ‘Bartlett’ pear tree and ‘Kieffer’ pear tree, available from Garden Goods Direct, are partially self-fertile, although they generally produce better crops with a suitable pollination partner. Kieffer also offers good resistance to fire blight, making it worth considering in areas where this disease is a concern.

November can be a good time to plant a bare-root pear tree in milder regions. The plant is dormant, but its root system can continue to grow during the winter as long as the soil remains sufficiently warm and unfrozen. It is also possible to plant container trees in November. Be sure the planting hole is several times as wide as the root system, but no deeper than the root ball.

If you want a tree with sweet, juicy fruit, consider planting a plum tree. The fruit is delicious when eaten fresh, but also makes great compotes or jams. Plum trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 4–9, depending on the variety. November is a good month to plant bare-root plum trees in milder regions, and it’s suitable for container-grown plum trees as well. Just don’t wait too long since you can't plant after the ground is frozen. In colder zones, spring planting is often safer.

Most fruit trees need sunny locations, and plum trees are not an exception. In fact, it’s particularly important to select a good site since plums flower very early in spring. If your tree is in a low-lying frost pocket, the blossoms will be vulnerable to late frosts. You should also pick a site that offers protection from harsh winds. Plant your plum in cool, well-draining soil. Wet, heavy soil can lead to root disease.

Most plum trees require a pollinator, so you’ll need to plant two compatible trees. However, several varieties are self-fertile, so a single tree is enough to produce a harvest. One great option is the ‘Methley’ plum tree, available from Trees.com, which produces sweet, juicy fruit without needing a pollination partner.

Most of us know that a peach tree is a deciduous tree with juicy round fruits. Here’s a lesser-known fact: the same botanical species can grow fuzzy fruits, called peaches, or glossy-skinned fruits, called nectarines. Peach trees generally thrive in USDA hardiness zones 5–8, although this varies by variety. Peach trees, especially bare-root peach trees, can be successfully planted in November, as long as the ground is not frozen. In colder regions, however, spring planting is often safer.

Peach trees need sunny sites. Plant yours where it will get at least 6–8 hours a day of direct sun. This is essential to trigger flower buds and sweeten the fruit. The soil should be well-draining since standing water will rot the tree’s roots. If the tree is grafted, be sure to set the tree in the planting hole so that the graft union sits above the soil line.

Peach trees also need a specific amount of winter cold, chill hours, when temperatures fall within the range of approximately 32°F to 45°F (0°C to 7°C). Standard peach varieties need from 650 to 1,050 chill hours, although you can find low-chill types that need as few as 100 hours.

One great option for colder regions is the ‘Red Haven’ peach tree from Trees.com, a self-fertile variety that produces sweet, juicy peaches and needs around 800–900 chill hours. For warmer regions with mild winters, try ‘Tropic Snow,’ a low-chill variety that needs just 225 chill hours and produces deliciously sweet, white-fleshed peaches.

The American persimmon is among our most overlooked native fruit trees. This species does not get the spotlight given to apple, peach, or pear trees, yet it offers so much: edible fruit, wildlife habitat, and attractive fall foliage. The fruit is an important food source for wild birds and mammals, including raccoons, opossums, and foxes, and it remains available into early winter, when many other food sources have diminished.

Native to the eastern and southeastern United States, these trees are very cold-hardy, thriving in USDA hardiness zones 4–9. You can buy a common American persimmon tree from Plant Addicts to enjoy its fruit and seasonal interest in your own backyard. American persimmons typically have separate male and female trees, but some varieties are self-fertile and can produce fruit without a pollination partner. If you're growing a tree for its fruit, check its pollination requirements before buying.

The trees can grow to between 35 and 60 feet (10–18 m) tall, although they can be kept smaller by pruning. The fruit they produce is orange and initially astringent, but it becomes sweet and delicious when it fully ripens, often around the time of the first frost.

November is a good time to plant an American persimmon tree in milder regions. You cannot plant at this time, however, if the ground is frozen. Find a well-drained area with loamy, organically rich soil in a full sun location. Avoid frost pockets since these trees may be damaged by unseasonable frosts.

Fig trees have a long and somewhat exotic history. They have been cultivated for 12,000 years and are among the earliest domesticated plants. They have deep symbolic meaning as symbols of peace and prosperity, but, perhaps more important to modern gardeners, the trees are tough, drought-tolerant, and resistant to pests and diseases.

Fig trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 6–11, depending on the variety, although those in colder zones may need winter protection. For a reliable, sweet-fruited variety, try the ‘Brown Turkey’ fig from Nature Hills, which is well suited to milder regions. Gardeners in colder zones might prefer the ‘Chicago Hardy’ fig, also available from Nature Hills, which can withstand much lower winter temperatures with suitable protection. Both varieties are self-fruitful, so you only need one tree to enjoy a harvest.

If you live in USDA zone 8 or above, it is generally appropriate to plant your tree in November, provided the ground isn't frozen. In cooler zones, you should wait until spring. For November planting, select a full-sun location, ideally against a south- or southwest-facing wall. This helps the tree capture and retain warmth. The soil must be well-draining and slightly acidic. Water the tree deeply right after planting to settle the soil around the roots.

Once the tree is planted, apply a layer of organic mulch around the base, keeping the mulch a few inches away from the actual trunk to prevent rot.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7891. Bored, Overtired, or Just Being a Dog? What Makes Puppies Hyper

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Puppyhood is a huge learning curve â for both owner and dog â and managing a puppyâs energy can be one of the hardest parts of it. Hyperactivity is common, and the good news is that knowing what causes it makes it much easier to help a puppy calm down. The reasons range from ordinary puppy exuberance to, on rare occasions, a health problem.

Puppies burn energy by exploring and playing, but they can run out of things to do. A mix of toys, activities, and walks helps manage their energy. Without it, boredom and frustration can lead to destructive behavior or aggression, or to zooming around the house. A puppy with no good outlet, such as a sturdy chew toy, will release that pent-up energy by barking, running around, or jumping on people.

The opposite problem is just as real. Just like toddlers who throw tantrums when theyâre overtired, puppies that have too much going on can become hyperactive because they donât understand that they need a nap, and the discomfort frustrates them. Finding the balance gets easier as an owner learns a puppyâs energy levels. Plenty of activities and training sessions help, as do regular quiet times for cooling off and a quick nap to recharge.

Puppies learn quickly, and that includes behaviors that owners donât mean to encourage. If a puppy gets attention every time it becomes overexcited during play, even when the owner is trying to say stop, the puppy sees it as a reward, and the next time it feels neglected, hyper behavior may seem like a good way to get noticed. The fix is to interact when the puppy is gentle or relaxed, and to become less interesting when it gets overexcited, by dropping the tug toy and stepping away.

All puppies have energy, but the amount varies by breed, and a breedâs original purpose matters as much as its size. Border Collies, bred to herd sheep all day, require lots of physical and mental stimulation to keep up with their boundless energy. A more sedate breed, like the French Bulldog or King Charles Spaniel, tends to have far less energy to burn. A Border Collie puppy has less stamina than an adult, but it still has plenty of energy to manage.

Food affects everything from digestion to brain development, and it can influence sleep cycles, energy levels, and skin health. The wrong diet may contain too much of certain ingredients, often protein, which can lead to hyperactivity. Researching a puppyâs nutritional needs and checking the ingredients with a vet is worthwhile.

Obedience training teaches a dog how to manage its behavior, and socialization helps it get used to people, other pets, and new situations. Without them, a puppy doesnât know how to react, and a quick play session can end with an overexcited puppy that canât calm down. A tiny puppy climbing on people or nipping fingers may seem cute, but puppies donât always stay small, and an adult dog that bites or jumps can be dangerous, especially around a child or a stranger.

Most of the time, hyperactivity is easily corrected and comes down to diet, breed, or limited exercise. Health problems are a rare cause. If a puppy is still hyper after changes to diet, activity, and training, a vet check to rule out any health issues is always a good idea. The earlier a problem is diagnosed, the easier it is to treat.

Puppies are still learning what their bodies are telling them. One of the most common signs is becoming hyper or restless when they need to go. An older puppy getting used to house training may be asking to go out, while a younger one may not understand the signal and burst into a case of the zoomies until it figures it out.

Most hyperactivity simply comes from being a puppy. Younger dogs are more excitable, and they need lots of energy to explore the world without yet knowing how to manage it. Puppies steadily grow out of it. They may still get the zoomies later on, but they settle and learn better control. Rewarding calm behavior, working on obedience, and giving a working breed a job to do all help.

Researching a breed before bringing a puppy home matters, since a high-energy herding breed can be too much for some households. Time matters too, because a long workday followed by evening chores may leave little room for the exercise a puppy needs.

Activity is the best way to manage energy, and it shouldnât be only physical. Puzzles and other mental activities keep a brain busy as well. Calm behavior deserves rewards with treats and attention, and disengaging when a puppy gets overexcited teaches that playing nicely keeps the game going longer. Training helps too, because some hyper behavior is really bad manners learned along the way, such as jumping up or racing around when the leash comes out.

Most puppies grow out of their boundless energy as they reach adulthood and learn self-control, which can take between one and two years depending on breed. Some breeds are naturally quieter and happier to laze around, while more active breeds never lose their energy. A routine tailored to a dogâs needs is essential, along with choosing a puppy that suits the family.

A puppyâs energy can come from exuberance, overstimulation, tiredness, boredom, diet, or, on rare occasions, health issues. Working out which one applies, and adjusting the daily schedule to match, is the key to keeping it manageable.

This easy DIY combines rose hips, seed heads, and garden foliage to create a beautiful natural decoration that's a treat for winter birds, too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Seasonal wreaths are popular décor for the front door, porches, patios, and decks. Stores offer a lot of options, from plastic wreaths to pricier products made from natural materials. But why spend money on these? Your backyard likely contains almost everything you need to make your own holiday wreath.

And while you’re crafting a gorgeous natural wreath, why not help birds in winter? Backyard birds have far fewer natural resources to exploit in the cold, so any support you can provide benefits these garden friends. By being thoughtful about what you put in your natural wreath, you can enjoy seasonal décor and support birds.

Making a winter wreath for birds that is also beautiful isn’t difficult. Here's what you’ll need and how to put it all together to make a bird feeder wreath you can display all year. And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then don't miss our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

The first step in making a wreath is to gather materials. You’ll want evergreen cuttings for the wreath's foundation, plus attractive decorative items that also feed birds. Avoid any plants that have been treated with pesticides. You can make an exclusively rose hip wreath or seed head wreath, or mix and match elements within one wreath. Here’s what to look for in the garden:

The foundation of your wreath will be a base made from the flexible stems and sticks you gathered. You’ll also need twine or florist wire, like this Pauleen wire, and pruning shears or sharp, sturdy scissors. If you are short on time or materials, you can also buy a willow or grapevine base at a craft or garden store – this 14-Inch Grapevine Wreath from Amazon is ideal. Making your own isn’t difficult, though:

Don’t worry about making your wreath perfectly symmetrical. You can hide some flaws with the added elements.

This is the creative part of the project. Exactly where and how you add the decorative elements is up to you, but start with evergreens:

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

How you arrange the elements is totally up to your taste and creative mood. You can do a wreath loaded with rose hips or with a little bit of everything arranged so that you can still see a lot of the evergreens. As you design your wreaths, consider both aesthetics and how birds will use it. Avoid synthetic décor, like glitter or plastic berries, which could also harm birds.

Your wreath is holiday décor, but it’s also for the birds, so find somewhere to hang it where they can find it and feed safely on it. A sheltered position is best to protect birds from strong winds and predators. It should also be visible, so birds can find it, not too tucked away. If it is more out in the open, place the wreath near a sheltered area, so birds can quickly dart between the wreath and shelter.

It’s also important to consider window safety. You might want the wreath in a spot you can see from inside, but don’t place it so close to windows that birds risk a deadly collision.

A bird feeder wreath might start out as Christmas décor, but it can offer visual interest and feed all winter if you take good care of it:

A holiday wreath can be so much more than a temporary piece of Christmas decoration. Decorate for the entire winter with a natural wreath that also supports your local wildlife. Gather from your own garden and talk to neighbors if you need more materials. Experiment with any natural food source in your area, from various berries and rose hips to all kinds of seedheads and pinecones. And then, enjoy the show.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

#7888. How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

If you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers. Edible plants can bring striking foliage, flowers, fruit, and structure to a container, even when producing a harvest isn’t the primary goal.

As a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses. It’s no different when composing a container or a grouping of containers. For now, set aside flavor and look at their other sensory qualities: visual appeal, fragrance, texture, and even the sounds of foliage and seed heads moving in the wind.

Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell

Successful container design balances aesthetics with the growing needs of individual plants. Before exploring specific edimentals—plants valued for both their edible and ornamental qualities—consider a few practical guidelines.

Growing vegetables in containers demands certain conditions if you want a good harvest. But when appearance takes priority over production, you can make different choices. For instance, allowing lettuce and other leafy greens to bolt can introduce interesting flower stalks and seed heads, even though the leaves may become bitter and less desirable for eating.

Containers give you greater control over growing conditions, but plants still need the right light, moisture, and soil. Choose edible varieties that tend to be compact, dwarf, bush, or well-behaved vines or climbers.

It’s helpful to choose the largest container your budget and space will allow. Larger pots generally provide more room for roots and retain moisture longer, while smaller containers dry out more quickly and may require more frequent watering and feeding. Mixing container sizes also adds visual interest to a display. Whatever the size, make sure the container has adequate drainage.

One advantage of container gardening is the ability to tailor the soil to your plants’ needs. Start with a quality potting mix and choose plants with similar preferences for drainage, moisture, and soil acidity. This flexibility also lets you grow plants that might struggle in your native garden soil.

Because container plants depend on a limited volume of soil, they may need supplemental fertilizer as nutrients become depleted. Think about what you’re trying to encourage: Excess nitrogen, for example, can promote leafy growth at the expense of flowers or fruit. Choose a fertilizer appropriate for your plants, follow label directions, and consult your local nursery or Extension service for specific recommendations.

Mulch helps regulate soil temperature and retain moisture, even in containers. For open compositions where the soil surface is visible, use decorative materials such as small pine cones, shells, buckwheat hulls, or gravel. Leaf mold and finely shredded bark work well, too. Apply a shallow layer that allows water to pass through, and keep mulch away from plant crowns and stems.

Use what you have and think about growing your own. Many vegetables are quite easy to start from seed. Growing your own is both economical and a way to reduce the need for purchased transplants, especially when you use peat-free soil mixes. Choosing peat-free mixes can also help reduce demand for peat extracted from carbon-storing wetlands. Collect rainwater where permitted for an additional irrigation source. Avoid using untreated household gray water on edible crops. Incorporating perennials also extends the life of your displays. They can be combined with seasonal plants or relocated elsewhere in the garden when a container needs refreshing.

The ever-popular Thriller-Filler-Spiller container method holds its ground because of its snappy moniker and reliable formula. In this method, the thriller is the dramatic focal point; the filler is a bushy, mid-level plant or plants; and the spiller—wait for it—spills over the edge of the container. It’s an easy enough recipe that most people can create something attractive, but truthfully, many fail to think much about what they are combining, which results in the big-box special: a nondescript spiky grass towering over a showy fuchsia, with invasive creeping Jenny (Lysimachia nummularia, Zones 3–9) trailing out.

We can do better. While perhaps less catchy, think about composing your container much like you might a landscape. Consider structure (the framework); form and habit (the shape); spatial orientation (how it reads visually—does the plant have a horizontal, vertical, or some other orientation?); visual texture (is the foliage fine, coarse, or medium?); and color (is it intense, receding, or something else?). Go beyond appearance and consider the full range of sensory experience: how plants move in the wind and what that sounds like, what they smell like, and how they feel when brushed up against.

Not every plant or combination will hit all the notes, so don’t stress. Focus on a few complementary qualities. Combine the plants in your container to create contrasts or enhance similarities. Look at leaf, bloom, and seed head form. The idea is to create layers—low, mid, and upper—and aim for three to five plants that play off each other’s traits within the container.

Are you trying to create something formal, informal, transitional, organic, or eclectic? Knowing how you want your container to read to the viewer can help you make choices about which edible plants may be a better addition to the mix.

When composing your containers, don’t forget to look beyond edimentals. Often the best containers mix edible plants with purely ornamental plants, such as leafy or flowering perennials and small shrubs. The juxtaposition of disparate plants usually determines a container’s success—different textures, colors, heights, and forms.

While incorporating disparate elements creates visual interest, it’s also important to give the eye somewhere to rest. A collection of pots filled with different plant combinations can feel jarring without repetition or quieter areas to balance the display.

A repeat may be exactly what it sounds like: using the same plant or using the same color, form, or texture across pots. Areas to pause are pots that may contain one uniform element—such as like plants, colors, or containers.

Another approach is to view the containers as individual components. Rather than composing containers with several different kinds of plants (including vegetables, of course), try grouping containers that each have one type of plant. This can be a powerful display akin to naturalistic block-style planting design.

Sometimes a container needs more. Perhaps it needs some staking for a vine, or simply a bit of additional texture. Incorporate natural materials such as pruned branches (dry or living), fallen branches covered in lichen, wild berry clusters, pine cones, grape or hop vines, dried elements such as grasses, or even small stumps.

And don’t neglect the value of seed heads—just because that kale bloom has now passed doesn’t necessarily mean you want to remove the plant; wait to see those prolific little yellow pods. And a radish gone to seed showcases its most redeeming feature: crunchy seed clusters that rattle in the wind!

By definition, a container is simply a receptacle for holding goods or objects, so feel free to think beyond the pots you find at the nursery. Salvaged and vintage items work well combined with more traditional terra-cotta pots. Take a high-low approach and use found items from your own home along with a special planter from a boutique garden center.

Don’t forget these irreverent options can also be repurposed in unexpected applications—that antique copper colander can go on to lead a new life as a hanging basket. Just make sure repurposed containers provide adequate drainage and are suitable for growing food if you plan to harvest from them.

One of the biggest benefits of working with containers is the opportunity to modify them by adding or removing plants to capture the best seasonal foliage. While many edibles are annuals that end their season late in the year, others produce seed heads or even a second flush after cutback.

Some common edible members of the carrot family (Apiaceae), including carrots (Daucus carota, biennial); parsnips (Pastinaca sativa, biennial); parsley (Petroselinum crispum, biennial); and celery and celeriac (Apium graveolens, biennial), produce flowers in their second growing season. Their delicate foliage and umbrella-shaped flower clusters add texture and attract pollinators. Deep-rooted crops such as carrots and parsnips need sufficiently deep containers, particularly if you plan to leave them in place for a second season.

Osage orange (Maclura pomifera, Zones 4–9) isn’t a citrus fruit at all. This North American native tree produces large, greenish yellow, orange-like fruits with a distinctive, bumpy surface. Although the fruits aren’t considered edible, their unusual appearance and citrus-like fragrance make them wonderful decorative accessories for autumn container displays.

Another lesser-known edible is a well-known perennial: ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris, Zones 2–8). Its tightly coiled young fronds, known as fiddleheads, are harvested as a spring delicacy before unfurling into the familiar feathery foliage.

Lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina, Zones 3–8) offers similarly beautiful emerging fronds for ornamental containers, but it should not be treated as an interchangeable edible. Many ferns contain potentially harmful compounds, so accurate identification is essential. Only properly identified ostrich fern fiddleheads should be eaten, and they must be thoroughly cooked. For more information, see the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s guide to fiddlehead safety. Of course, you can simply enjoy their fascinating emerging foliage up close in a container.

Vegetables that you may not have thought about embracing in your ornamental containers include okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, annual), with its large pods and hibiscus-like flowers; artichokes, such as ‘Purple Italian Globe’ (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus ‘Purple Italian Globe’, Zones 7–10), with dramatic silvery foliage and purple flower heads (use your largest container); cucamelon (Melothria scabra, annual), also called mouse melon, which resembles a tiny watermelon on a prolific climbing vine; and leafy greens of all sorts. Look out for the striking edible red-veined dock (Rumex sanguineus, Zones 5–8), with the unpalatable common name, bloody dock—it’s a stunner. Its green leaves are marked with vivid red veins, and the young foliage is edible in moderation, although it contains oxalic acid.

More common edibles with uncommon traits include delicate currant tomatoes such as ‘Sweet Pea’ (Solanum pimpinellifolium ‘Sweet Pea’, annual) or compact tomatoes such as ‘Tiny Tim’ (Solanum lycopersicum ‘Tiny Tim’, annual).

Alpine strawberries (Fragaria vesca, Zones 4–9) come in a range of colors from white and pale yellow to pink and red, depending on the selection. These diminutive berries add character and spill over the edge of containers.

Peppers such as the teardrop ‘Biquinho Red’ (Capsicum chinense ‘Biquinho Red’, annual) are eye-catching and tolerant of many conditions. Compact blueberry (Vaccinium cvs., Zones 3–8) foliage glows red in the autumn, acting as a foil for its partners.

And there are so. Many. More. Whatever you’re interested in, you can find an edimental that will fill that niche.

Edible plants offer a broader palette that many gardeners and designers overlook—choosing them for containers broadens your range of plant materials and, most importantly, creates opportunities for delight and intrigue when used in unexpected ways.

They also make it possible to garden in small spaces or places where in-ground planting isn’t practical. Containers can be moved to improve growing conditions, rearranged to create a new focal point, or grouped to screen an unwanted view. They also let you accommodate plants that might struggle in your native soil or spread too aggressively in garden beds, such as mint (Mentha cvs., Zones 3–9) or sunchokes (Helianthus tuberosus, Zones 3–9). Just be sure to give vigorous plants enough room to grow.

In the eastern United States, ornamental kales and cabbages, paired with mums, are a common sight this time of year. While there is nothing inherently wrong with them, now you know you have more edimental options, so why not experiment with a wider range of edible plants? From colorful leafy greens to fruiting vines and impressive seed heads, there’s no shortage of possibilities for creating containers that look as interesting as the plants themselves.

And for more Northeast regional reports, click here.

Heather Tuckman is a garden designer and owner of Resilient Ground Design in southeastern Pennsylvania. She combines her background in horticulture, garden design, and psychology to create beautiful, ecologically thoughtful landscapes.

#7887. War Dogs of History: Chips

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, New York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

Chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

Chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, quickly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the company commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

In 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

Washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

In January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

Chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

Among the dogs of the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record. Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Morgan Farr is a writer, graphic designer, and advocate who has spent her career telling the stories of working dogs and the people who love them. She serves as the Social Media Coordinator for both the Military Working Dog Heritage Museum and the National Service Animals Monument. She previously served as the social media manager for the U.S. Army Military Working Dog Program.

Together with her husband, an Army veterinarian, Morgan co-founded Canine Advancement Group, which offers education on canine wellness and welfare for both working and companion dogs. She is a member of the American Veterinary Medical History Society, the American Historical Association, the American Association for State and Local History, and the Society for Military History. In 2025, she was named the Armed Forces Insurance Military Spouse of the Year for Joint Base San Antonio.

At home, Morgan is a military spouse, a homeschooling mother of four, a small business owner of Dog-Eared Press, and a co-op instructor. She shares her household with a high-drive Dutch Shepherd and a spirited Bombay cat, who remind her daily that every animal, working or companion, deserves understanding, partnership, and thoughtful care.

Despite its compact size, it still puts out enough heat to warm a 1,200-square-foot room.

The stove consists of plated-steel construction with a cast-iron door that features a large glass window to provide a nice view of the burning logs. Despite its small size, the door is wide enough to handle logs up to 18 inches long. A brushed-nickel handle on the loading door and ash drawers add an elegant look to this rustic wood stove.

Get the Ashley Hearth 1,200-square-foot wood stove at Lowe’s.

We considered numerous criteria when narrowing the field of wood stoves to these top selections. A wood stove’s ability to produce heat is key, so we only considered models that could provide heat for 900 square feet of space or more (except for the portable and camping categories).

Since the visible flames are a large part of a wood stove’s appeal, we mainly selected models that provide a good view of the firebox with large windows on the doors. Build quality is crucial, so we only chose models with higher-gauge steel construction and forged-iron doors, except for our upgrade pick, which uses soapstone.

Understanding the two types of wood stoves, the materials used to make them, and their heating capacity are all vital when shopping for one of these appliances. Ahead, learn more about these and other important attributes of the best wood stoves.

Wood stoves are available in two types: catalytic and noncatalytic. Catalytic wood stoves differ from noncatalytic in that they produce fewer exhaust fumes and burn more efficiently. In addition to burning wood, catalytic wood stoves also have a combustor that burns smoke and byproducts. This design allows the stove to burn cleaner with a slower burn rate, conserving fuel. Efficiency ratings for a catalytic wood stove range between 63 and 84 percent, making them ideal options for use as a primary source of heat.

Noncatalytic stoves are cheaper but not as efficient. They are better suited for use as a supplemental heater.

Most wood stoves are made from one of three materials: cast iron, plate steel, or soapstone. Cast iron, the most commonly used material, heats up quickly and retains warmth longer than other materials. However, it does crack more easily and is more expensive than other materials.

Plate steel, also a common material used in wood stoves, is durable and retains heat well, though not as well as cast iron. Soapstone is a high-end material for wood stoves. It retains heat better than cast iron, burns cleaner than other materials, and can burn for 24 hours or longer on a single load. Most wood stoves consist of either soapstone or plate steel with a cast-iron door.

A wood stove’s heating capacity determines how large of a space the wood stove can keep warm when it’s running with a full load of wood. The heating area for most stoves ranges from around 1,200 square feet for a small stove to as much as 2,200 square feet (or more) for a large model.

Keep in mind that, unlike a home’s central heating, which distributes heat through ductwork, a wood stove emanates heat from the fire, so the heat isn’t evenly distributed. The farther someone is from the wood stove, the cooler the temperature will be.

The heat output of a wood stove is measured in BTUs (British thermal units). Wood stoves range in BTU output from around 50,000 to 80,000 BTUs. The more BTUs, the greater the size of the space the wood stove can heat. A large 70,000-BTU wood stove can warm up to 2,200 square feet. While BTU level is a great indication of how powerful the stove is, not all manufacturers provide BTU information for their stoves.

A wood stove’s burn time is the amount of time one load of wood lasts before the stove requires reloading. Each stove’s burn time is determined by how much wood it can hold as well as the heat output of the stove, which can be regulated using the stove’s damper. The firewood type being used also affects burn time. Hardwoods burn more efficiently than softwood, which is less dense and therefore burns more quickly and at lower temperatures.

Wood-burning stoves produce toxic emissions; they create carbon monoxide, which can be deadly if not properly vented outside. Wood stoves are regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency, which performs safety tests on wood stoves to make sure they’re safe for consumer use. The emission limit for wood stoves is 2 grams to 2.5 grams per hour, depending on the type of wood. Catalytic stoves produce well under the EPA’s maximum, with emissions of around 0.5 grams per hour. Never buy a wood stove that is not certified by the EPA.

Perhaps the most important thing to consider when shopping for a wood stove is where it will go in the living space. Most freestanding wood stoves take up a significant chunk of real estate since they measure about 3 feet wide and 2 feet deep and require a buffer around them for safety. Portable models are much smaller—about 20 inches high and 10 inches deep and less than 40 pounds—allowing them to fit in the trunk of a car for a camping trip.

Keep in mind that the size of the stove also affects the size of wood they can burn. A standard freestanding or insert wood stove can hold logs up to 18 inches long, whereas portable models can typically handle logs that measure about 8 inches long.

In addition to providing a source of heat, wood stoves also create an ambience that’s similar to a wood-burning fireplace. Most wood stoves have glass windows that allow people sitting around the stove to watch the burning logs.

Some wood stoves also serve as a cooking stove, with flat tops that will support a frying pan or pot. Stoves with cooking functions are typically designed for outdoor use and camping trips.

The best place for a wood stove is as close to the center of the area requiring heat as possible. This allows the stove to radiate warmth in all directions, better heating the space.

Hardwoods—which include oak, maple, ash, and birch—are the best-burning woods. They will burn longer and hotter than softwoods like pine and also contain the least amount of pitch and sap inside of them.

Use a brush to sweep up any debris or ash that was not collected by the fireplace’s ash pan. Next, use a wire brush to clean off any buildup inside the flue pipe. Wipe off the exterior of the wood stove with a dry cloth. Be sure to avoid using liquids, which can leave streaks.

The average wood stove should last between 10 and 20 years, depending on usage and care.

It is safe to leave a wood fireplace on overnight, as long as you follow a few precautions. Allow the wood to burn for a few hours before going to bed. Before turning in for the night, add ash to the burning logs to dampen the flames and slow the burning process. Next, close the stove air vents to reduce the size of the fire, ensuring it will be safe even when burning through the night.

Yes. If the indoor wood-burning stove is not properly vented to the outside of the home, it can cause exhaust fumes to collect inside the home, resulting in carbon monoxide poisoning. If a wood-burning stove is installed properly, vented to the outside of the home, and EPA certified, it is safe to use.

After Testing 20 Air Purifiers, We Found One That Does Something the Rest Can’t

Same functionality, different package? Not with this Sans air purifier, which offers more advanced filtration and features than most models I’ve tested—without a premium price tag.

We didn’t test LED lights exclusively but focused strongly on that type.

To begin our testing, we hung the string lights and left them in place for several days. After dark, we attempted to read or perform other activities—such as grilling—with just the illumination from the lights. We used a testing rubric, scoring each product based on illumination, light quality, and overall ambience. If the string lights were marketed as shatterproof, we dropped them on a concrete patio from head height to see if they would crack. For the ones advertised as waterproof, we left them out in a rainstorm or sprayed them with water. Then, we tested them again after they dried. We noted the cord’s length, the number of bulb sockets, and how easy they were to hang.

A simple strand of string lights can transform a plain backyard into an inviting outdoor space. Compared with many other types of exterior house lights, string lights are among the most affordable and easiest to install. If you want to hang string lights outdoors, consider light type, size and shape, brightness, and color. A weather-resistant design, a lengthy cord, and a remote or app control can make the lights safer and easier to use.

Most outdoor string lights feature LED, incandescent, solar, or battery-operated bulbs. Each type varies in durability, energy efficiency, and lifespan. When shopping for outdoor string lights, consider which type of lighting is most suitable for the space.

Since outdoor string lights are exposed to the elements, it’s important to select a set that can withstand rainy conditions and heavy gusts of wind. It’s inconvenient to take the string lights down every time inclement weather is forecast.

First, check the product description to determine if the lights are intended for outdoor use. Using indoor lighting outside creates a potential fire hazard. Second, make sure the product is water-resistant (or waterproof, as even spots under a porch or gazebo roof can grow damp in bad weather). Weather-resistant lights can handle direct exposure to water and feature watertight seals to protect their interior components from accumulating moisture and causing safety issues.

String light bulbs are available in a variety of styles and shapes, which can give the strands a unique aesthetic.

According to Friedman, “You’ll also want to look for shatterproof bulbs, ideally LED, since they’re cooler and more efficient.”

When choosing a bulb size, consider the available outdoor space, ease of installation, and desired look.

Small bulbs are a good pick for small outdoor spaces or garden lighting; they won’t overpower a space or other outdoor decorations. These bulbs are generally more subtle, providing gentle background lighting. They provide less light and are commonly chosen for decorative purposes.

Large bulbs are more striking and offer a bolder look. Their larger size can provide more direct illumination. Generally brighter, they’re well suited to larger spaces that need more lighting. Large decorative bulbs, such as globe bulbs and Edison bulbs, can make a style statement.

Keep in mind that bulb size can affect installation. String lights with small bulbs are generally lightweight and easier to maneuver. They may be easier to install than string lights with larger, heavier, and bulkier bulbs.

Most globe outdoor string light bulbs come in one of three bulb sizes:

Most Edison-style string light bulbs are an S14 bulb size, which is a medium-size, oval-shaped bulb that’s 32 millimeters (just over 1.25 inches) in diameter.

When it comes to the appearance of outdoor string lights, brightness and color temperature are two of the most important factors to consider.

Lumens measure the amount of light output from a bulb—the more lumens, the brighter the bulb. When deciding on bulb brightness, take into account the desired lighting effect. String light bulbs can range from 5 to more than 100 lumens per bulb. Users often choose string lights for their glowy appearance rather than their brightness, so lower lumens often do just fine to set the mood. Lumens are different from wattage, as wattage measures how much power a bulb consumes and not necessarily how bright a light appears.

Lighting color temperature is measured using the Kelvin temperature scale. This scale measures how warm or cool the light appears. Lower numbers on the Kelvin scale look warmer, and higher numbers look cooler.

Most home lighting falls between 2000K and 6000K. Bulbs around 2700K have a cozy, warm white color with a yellow hue, while bulbs over 5000K offer stark, crisp lighting with a blue hue. Warm lighting makes a space look more cozy and inviting, while cool lighting can often appear harsh, especially at night. For this reason, warmer bulbs are generally preferred for ambient outdoor lighting.

Outdoor string lights typically come in lengths of 10, 25, 35, 50, and 100 feet. When choosing the ideal wire length, consider the size of the outdoor space and the lighting layout.

Patio string lights can outline garden borders, wrap around banisters and trees, or suspend over seating spaces. The best way to determine the necessary wire length is to use a piece of twine to measure where the lights will go. If the lights require corded power, make sure to include enough length to reach the outlet, or keep an extension cord handy.

To line one side of an average balcony or small porch, a 10-foot string of outdoor patio lights may do the trick. A small 8-foot-long by 6-foot-wide patio space typically requires 25 to 50 feet of string lighting. A medium 12-foot-square outdoor space may need 50 to 100 feet of string lighting, depending on the desired layout. For more spacious areas or to illuminate a large event, more than 100 feet of string lighting is usually necessary.

In terms of wire strength, Friedman recommends commercial-grade stringers with heavy-gauge wire. “This will hold tension much better, and the extra insulation will provide safety and durability.” He adds that “these stringers are much heavier than your average consumer string lights, so make sure you mount them securely.”

For those who want to upgrade from basic string lights, consider a product with extra features like color-changing bulbs, dimming options, and remote control or app operation. As we discovered in our tests, users are able to create entirely different moods by selecting different bulb colors.

String lights can instantly transform a typical yard or patio into a warm and inviting space, but choosing the right set of lights is a must for creating the desired atmosphere. White light is the most effective lighting color since it is closest to natural light. Warm white lights have a cozy, inviting yellow tinge, making them a popular pick for outdoor lighting. Colorful bulbs are often chosen for the ambience they create rather than their lighting ability. These lights add a decorative flair and can be a fun addition for different seasons and holidays.

#7883. Eco-Friendly Hardscaping Ideas for a More Sustainable Garden

The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

With 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

Some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis

Conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

Finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

Of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

Patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, new pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is important to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

Repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

It’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available new materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

Whether you’re planning a new patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

You'd best believe that Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse's favorite houseplant is far fancier than your average spider plant, folks...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse are fast becoming the it couple of the moment (not least of all because the man formerly known as Edward Cullen is now Bond, James Bond). So you'd best believe they're setting trends left, right, and center – even in the world of indoor gardening.

And while we'd expect the pair to have a suitably impressive garden, it turns out their houseplant of choice is considerably more interesting than your average monstera or spider plant. In fact, it's a miniature tree with a rather sophisticated reputation: the not-so-humble bonsai!

Yes, with the couple's busy schedules taking them between different homes and locations, it makes sense that they're all about the idea of bringing greenery indoors. After all, houseplants offer a lovely way to make a space feel personal, even when you're not necessarily putting down roots for the long term. And if you're going to invest in an indoor plant, then why not make it something a little more unusual?

Speaking to the Perfectly Imperfect Newsletter in September 2024, Suki Waterhouse revealed that she developed a rather unexpected obsession with bonsai trees during the final month of her pregnancy.

'When I was preggers in the last month and didn’t really feel like seeing anyone, I got obsessed with getting a bonsai tree,' she says. 'I found a number on Google and pulled up to a house in East Hollywood and a lady had a bunch of them locked up in her back garden. Felt super cool and mysterious. Some of them she’d had for 30 years. Fell in love with this guy and have become obsessed with pruning.'

The leaves on this bonsai fold up at night or in subdued light, and it wakes up when we do!

It's a wonderfully specific plant obsession, and one we can absolutely get behind. Especially as there's something rather magical about a tiny tree that's been carefully cultivated for decade; there's a reason that bonsai is as much an art form as it is a gardening hobby.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Of course, Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson aren't the only ones who appreciate the appeal of the beautiful bonsai tree. In fact, there's been something of a growing appreciation for the slower, more mindful side of gardening, and bonsai? Why, that fits the philosophy rather beautifully.

More importantly? Well, despite the fact that bonsai trees have a reputation for being (whisper it) high-maintenance, they're not as intimidating as their appearance might suggest. The trick is choosing the right one – so look for a variety suited to indoor conditions and make a note of its basic requirements. And, as Suki herself pointed out, a little regular pruning and thoughtful watering can go a long way.

If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have inspired you to introduce a little bonsai magic into your own home, there are a few varieties worth considering...

If you're new to bonsai, ficus is arguably the best place to start. These tropical trees are considerably more forgiving than many traditional bonsai varieties and adapt well to indoor conditions. Their glossy leaves and interesting roots make them particularly striking, too.

Give something like this Small Ficus Live Bonsai Tree from Brussell's Bonsai a bright position with plenty of indirect light, keep it away from cold draughts and water when the top layer of compost begins to dry.

If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have got you in the mood for something a little more unusual, consider the Hawaiian umbrella tree (Schefflera arboricola).

This bonsai's distinctive leaves and naturally branching growth make it a particularly attractive choice for an indoor plant.

It's also relatively tolerant of indoor humidity levels and can cope with slightly less-than-perfect light conditions, although a bright spot will always help it thrive. Take care to allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings, and prune regularly to maintain its shape.

A lovely option for anyone who tends to be a little forgetful with watering, jade bonsai (Crassula ovata) is a succulent that enjoys plenty of bright light and needs much less frequent watering than tropical bonsai varieties.

Pick up something like this Live Jade from Brussell's Bonsai, let the compost dry out thoroughly between waterings, and make sure it's planted in a free-draining bonsai mix to prevent its roots from sitting in excess moisture.

Of course, even the most beginner-friendly bonsai isn't quite a plant you can forget about. Even Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse will tell you, light, watering and occasional pruning are all important, and it's worth remembering that not every bonsai is suited to indoor living.

As a general rule of thumb, tropical and subtropical varieties are generally the best choice for growing inside; most traditional temperate trees need to experience the changing seasons outdoors.

Still, there's something rather lovely about the idea of tending to a little tree that could stay with you for decades. And if Suki Waterhouse's experience is anything to go by, it might just become your next very absorbing, very cool, very mysterious hobby.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

If you’re hosting holiday guests, it’s a good idea to take a walk through your home with fresh eyes. Is your home looking a little dingy, but you can’t put your finger on why? Touching up chipped or scratched paint on doors, baseboards, and other common areas of the home can refresh the whole zone. Use a narrow paint brush and leftover paint to cover blemishes, and your surfaces will look good as new.

When you are expecting a holiday houseful, you want to make sure your furnace is operating at peak efficiency. Swap in a top-quality furnace filter for cleaner air—and lower energy bills.

In testing, these motion-sensing lights reacted the quickest and most consistently—and were among the easiest to install.  Read our full review.

The first goal of hosting a party: Make sure guests find your home. Install a solar-powered house number that is nice and bright after dark, and requires no upkeep on your part.

Bubble wrap and its thousands of insulating air pockets does a great job at protecting plants in pots from winter cold.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All year, I save up bubble wrap to use as a cheap DIY solution to see my garden through the winter. My trick is simple: I sandwich bubble wrap between a folded rectangle of burlap and wrap it around patio pots. Those little pockets of air act as excellent insulation, but my burlap and bubble-wrap pot-cozy does so much more than help to keep borderline-tender plants alive through winter.

If you're a fan of container gardening, you'll know that the temperature of soil in planters is so much more erratic than in the ground, leaving roots riding a right rollercoaster of conditions. By insulating pots, I save my plants a whole heap of stress, which means they can use their precious energy for far more exciting things. Winter-flowering pansies and violas in pots can stall in a cold snap, but stop that soil from freezing solid around their shallow roots and the plants will carry on pushing out their cheery petals. Winter-flowering heather in planters, too, will bloom far more steadily if their root balls are protected.

A DIY pot-wrap also helps to stop plants from drying out. When soil freezes – and it’ll freeze far sooner and deeper in a planter than in the ground – roots can’t access its moisture. If the plant keeps losing water through its leaves (and remember the wind strips moisture from foliage just as readily as the sun), it’s no different to drought conditions. And when a plant is losing more water than it can replace, it goes into survival mode. For early-flowering shrubs like Daphne odora and ornamental camellias, that can mean dropped buds and zero blooms.

Wrapping also helps to stop pots from cracking in the continual freeze-thaw of winter, especially if they're made from porous terracotta. And let’s not forget those borderline-hardy plants either: with their roots already safely insulated in bubble wrap and burlap in late fall, it’s a super-quick job to zip up shrubs in frost jackets when a cold spell is forecast.

It’s best to combine bubble wrap with good-quality, tightly-woven burlap on a roll such as this from Walmart to insulate pots. Cut a rectangle of burlap that’s twice the height of the pot and long enough to wrap all the way around with a generous overlap. Then fold the burlap in two and lay bubble wrap in between the two layers. Tie this around the pot with heavy-duty twine or rope, being careful not to cover the soil surface.

There are so many other uses for these low-cost materials as we head into winter:

Bubble wrap is so useful when winterizing your garden and, covered with a layer of burlap, looks pretty smart. I like to tie red ribbon around for the holidays, too, and my winter protection looks like Christmas decor! Re-using materials in your garden, whether you're recycling cardboard as a mulch or trying a few DIY upcycling projects to upgrade your garden storage, makes your garden budget go further, too.

#7879. GPOD on the Road: Shakespeare Garden in Evanston, Illinois

“O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”

Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!

Earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois. Today, we’re taking a look at another beautiful garden and a little Shakespearean history.

Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century! It all started in 1915, when the Garden Club of Evanston decided to create a garden to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death and celebrate the ties between England and America during World War I. They brought in renowned Danish-American landscape architect Jens Jensen to design the space, and by 1920, the club had completed planting a collection inspired by more than 50 plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s works. How neat! The garden was officially dedicated in 1930 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

The Garden Club of Evanston still cares for the garden today, and it’s a wonderful little place to visit. Enjoy!

While wandering the shady paths at the back of the garden, I came across this natural doorway formed by the trees. What a beautiful view of the central lawn and sundial! Jensen wanted the formal garden to feel like a clearing in the woods, and I think he achieved just that.

The garden measures just 70 by 100 feet and is made up of eight planting beds originally arranged in a formal knot-garden design. (If you’re not familiar with knot gardens, look them up! They’re amazing!) In 1990, English garden designer John Brookes recommended removing some of the boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) to make room for more perennials and a more relaxed planting style. He also had the sundial moved to the center to create a stronger focal point.

The garden underwent a renovation in 2016 to restore several of its historic features, including the wooden obelisks seen here, stone benches, and pathways. The project also included replacing declining plants to help preserve the original design.

My favorite view of the garden! Formally informal.

Jensen’s original planting list included everything from columbines (Aquilegia vulgaris, Zones 3–8) and violets (Viola spp., Zones 3–9) to poppies (Papaver somniferum, annual), peonies (Paeonia officinalis, Zones 4–8), and lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–8), all plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s writings. The plantings have changed over the years, but the garden still celebrates that connection.

Last, but certainly not least, this Elizabethan-style stone bench was installed in 1929, along with the garden’s memorial fountain. Nearly a century later, it’s still a beautiful spot to sit and enjoy the surroundings!

The Shakespeare Garden is open to the public, and I highly recommend stopping by if you’re ever in the area! You can learn more about its history and plan your visit through the Garden Club of Evanston’s website.
